THE MYTH OF A PERFECT TEEN SCHEDULE

In today's competitive world, teens are constantly seeking the perfect routine that balances university
applications, social life, extracurricular activities, family expectations, and eight hours of sleep. Many
turn to detailed planning as a way to solve their troubles, believing that there is one single “ideal” way
to organize their time. Their quest for this is fueled by peer pressure and competitive college
admissions. 5

However, what seems achievable in theory often ends up becoming a pressure cooker in
reality. A typical high schooler's day can stretch from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. All this time is spent with the
aim of securing a place at a good college. The first sacrifice on this path, along with many more to
come, is rest. Struggling to balance everything, deadlines, test preparation, and sports events, under
the pressure that every hour must be used "productively," teens leave little room for downtime, which 10
takes a toll on their mental and physical health.

A lot of the pressure comes from how much university entrance affects future opportunities,
yet not every teen has the same resources to follow an ideal schedule that helps to get into a good
institution. Finances, family circumstances, and heavy workloads make this goal achievable only for
some. Access to private tutoring, quiet study spaces, or extra academic programs can make a 15
significant difference, but these supports are not available to all students. Teens who have jobs or
family responsibilities are often at a disadvantage, and their struggles frequently go unrecognized.

For these underprivileged teens, failing to perform at their “best” can feel especially overwhelming,
particularly when compared to peers with more advantages.

A schedule that works effectively begins with identifying priorities, including non-negotiable 20
activities such as school, homework, family responsibilities, commutes, and meals. It also requires
paying attention to personal energy patterns, such as peak focus times and periods of fatigue, as well
as being aware of which tasks require the most mental effort. This helps to organize the schedule
efficiently by doing demanding work during high-energy hours and by leaving lighter tasks to be
completed during lower-energy periods. Extracurricular activities should be kept manageable and 25
include low-stress, enjoyable pastimes, such as music, walks, or socializing. Periods without
obligations provide rest and help prevent burnout. Teenagers have different rhythms and each
student should organize their time according to their own abilities and priorities.

30

                                WHAT DOES IT TAKE TO BE AN ASTRONAUT?

    In February 2021, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced it would be recruiting a new
    astronaut class, the first since 2008. It encouraged applicants from a broader spectrum of gender,
    physical ability, age, and ethnicity. My name is Kevin Fong and I decided to try. I also joined a
    WhatsApp group of like-minded hopefuls. There were 23,000 applicants. To be selected, you had
    to have a couple of degrees in science, preferably in different disciplines, with at least one at 5
    master's level or above.
          Against all odds, I made the smaller group of approximately 1,500 who went on to the next
    stage in Hamburg, Germany. We did classroom tests and video games: maths and physics
    quizzes, some psychometric screening and a bunch of fiendishly difficult pilot aptitude tests. The
    competitors in the room were impressive: intrepid oceanographers, particle physicists, military test 10
    pilots and Antarctic explorers, to list but a few. Given the calibre of my fellow applicants, I was
    shocked, some weeks later, to get a call for the next round of selection at the ESA Astronaut
    Centre in Cologne. Just 400 of us left.
          The testing day was brutal. Lengthy interrogations, psychological evaluations and 15
    professional parlour games followed, alone and in groups. The next round of testing was in
    Toulouse. I think I yelled out loud when I opened the invitation. Down to the final 91 now. At ESA's
    medical evaluation centre, the examination was exhaustive. To check our hearts, they made us
    run on a treadmill, hooked up to an electrocardiogram machine. I noticed that my heart was making
    abnormal beats. The medical team noticed them too. We exchanged uncomfortable glances. 20
    I hoped beyond hope that I might somehow sneak through. My email came around midday: a note
    thanking me for taking part but telling me that – for medical reasons beyond my control – I would
    go no further in the process. Game over.
          It was a hard process to fall out of, but my participation in the process of chasing the stars 25
    fuelled my ambitions in science and medicine and led to the career I continue to love here on
    Earth as a doctor. However, there is a bittersweet epilogue to this story that makes me feel sad.
    ESA trumpeted its intention to put diversity at the centre of this selection, but in this new astronaut
    class, there is – once again – an absence of ethnic diversity. It is a source of great sadness that
    a new generation of European children will gaze upon this latest ESA astronaut class without 30
    seeing themselves reflected.


   1. Answer these questions about the text in your own words (2 points, 1 each).

     a. Describe in your own words what happened to Kevin in Toulouse and what the consequences
     were.
     b. Why does Kevin feel sad?
 2. Read the following statements, decide whether they are true or false and justify your answer by
quoting evidence from the text (1 point, 0.50 each).

  a. During the selection process in Hamburg, the author competed against candidates from similar
  professional backgrounds.
  b. The author's experience with the ESA selection process had a positive impact on his current
  career path.


3. Find words or expressions in the text that mean the following (1 point, 0.25 each).

  a. Sharing similar opinions or goals (paragraph 1).
  b. Chances or probability of success in a certain undertaking (paragraph 2).
  c. Shouted loudly (paragraph 3).
  d. Look, stare (paragraph 4).


4. Rephrase FOUR of the following sentences beginning as shown (2 points, 0.5 each).

  a. The judges needed 18 months to complete the selection process.
  It took…………………………………………………………………………………………..

  b. Even though Kevin had difficulties, he didn't throw in the towel.
  Despite…………………………………………………………………………………………

  c. The agency should not allow any candidate with a heart condition to continue the training.
  Under no circumstances…….………………………………………………………………….

  d. The candidate didn’t make it to the second round because he did not speak languages.
  If………………………………………………………………………………………………..

  e. “Why don’t we repeat the ECG to be sure?” said the cardiologist.
  The cardiologist suggested …………………………………………………………………….

  f. It’s possible that the medical team was worried when they saw the ECG.
  The medical team might ……………………………………………………………………….


5. Write a composition of around 140-180 words on ONE of the following topics (4 points).

  a. You went through a selection process to become an astronaut and were eliminated. You believe
  the reasons for your elimination were unfair. Write a complaint letter to the selection committee
  explaining what happened and why you think it was unfair.
  b. Write an opinion essay on the importance of mental and physical strength for becoming an
  astronaut.
